hints: Focus on how solubility of Group 2 compounds changes down the group, it goes opposite ways for sulfates and hydroxides.
Remember that $\text{BaSO}_4$ is famously insoluble while $\text{MgSO}_4$ is very soluble, so test 1 with sulfate should give much more solid with barium.
Now flip the trend for test 2 with hydroxide, $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is sparingly soluble while $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is much more soluble, so link which ion gives more precipitate in each test.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two opposite solubility trends**

Think of Group 2 like a seesaw. Sulfates get less soluble as you go down, hydroxides get more soluble as you go down. This is the key to both tests.

**Analyse test 1 with sulfate ions**

We add $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ to $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. Since sulfates decrease in solubility down the group, barium sulfate is insoluble and magnesium sulfate is soluble.

$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) \text{ white precipitate}$$

So much more precipitate forms with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$.

**Analyse test 2 with hydroxide ions**

We add $\text{OH}^-$ to $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. Since hydroxides increase in solubility down the group, magnesium hydroxide is sparingly soluble and barium hydroxide is soluble.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) \text{ white precipitate}$$

So much more precipitate forms with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.

**Combine to choose the row**

Test 1: more with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. Test 2: more with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. That combination matches only one row in the table.

options.A: Test 1 is correct that $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ gives more precipitate, but test 2 is wrong. $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble, so $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ gives almost no precipitate with NaOH, not more.
options.B: Correct. Sulfates become less soluble down Group 2, so $\text{BaSO}_4$ precipitates while $\text{MgSO}_4$ stays in solution. Hydroxides become more soluble down Group 2, so $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ precipitates while $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ stays in solution.
options.C: Both parts are reversed. This comes from mixing up the trends, thinking sulfates get more soluble down the group and hydroxides get less soluble. In fact it is the opposite way round.
options.D: Test 2 is correct that $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ gives more precipitate, but test 1 is wrong. $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble, so $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ gives almost no precipitate with $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$, not more.
